content: Bell's palsy is a condition characterized by sudden, unilateral facial paralysis of unknown cause. It is diagnosed only when other potential causes of facial paralysis are excluded. The proposed mechanism involves swelling and entrapment of the facial nerve. Some surgeons have suggested that surgical decompression of the nerve might be a treatment option, ideally performed as soon as possible after the onset of symptoms. This review is an update of previous reviews published in 2011 and 2013, incorporating evidence from one newly identified study. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of surgical intervention in the early management of Bell's palsy. A comprehensive search was conducted on March 20, 2020, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP. Additionally, selected conference abstracts were hand-searched for relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that investigated any surgical intervention for Bell's palsy. Comparisons were made between surgical interventions and no treatment, delayed treatment (beyond three months), sham treatment, other surgical techniques, or medical treatments. Three authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data using standard Cochrane methodologies. The primary outcome was the complete recovery of facial palsy at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included recovery at three and six months, the presence of synkinesis or contracture at 12 months, psychosocial outcomes at 12 months, and any side effects or complications of treatment. Two trials, involving a total of 65 participants, met the inclusion criteria. One of these trials was newly identified in this update. The first study randomized 25 participants into surgical and non-surgical (no treatment) groups using statistical charts. However, one participant declined surgery, leaving 24 participants for evaluation. The second study quasi-randomized 53 participants, but only 41 were evaluable because 12 participants declined the intervention they were assigned. These 41 participants were divided into early surgery, late surgery, or non-surgical (no treatment) groups using an alternation method, though the method of alternation was not described. Neither study reported attempts to conceal allocation, and neither participants nor outcome assessors were blinded to the interventions. There were no losses to follow-up in the first study, but the second study lost three participants to follow-up, and 17 participants did not contribute to the assessment of secondary outcomes. Both studies were judged to have a high risk of bias. In both studies, surgeons used a retro-auricular/transmastoid approach to decompress the facial nerve. Regarding the primary outcome of complete recovery of facial palsy at 12 months, the evidence was highly uncertain. The first study reported no differences between the surgical and no-treatment groups. The second study provided numerical data but did not include statistical comparisons between groups for complete recovery. For the comparison of early surgery versus no treatment, the risk ratio (RR) was 0.76 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 11.11; P = 0.84; 33 participants), indicating no evidence of a difference. Similarly, for the comparison of early surgery versus late surgery, the RR was 0.47 (95% CI 0.03 to 6.60; P = 0.58; 26 participants). Both comparisons were based on very low-certainty evidence. Overall, the effects of surgery on facial nerve function at 12 months were considered very uncertain. The second study also reported adverse effects associated with surgery. There was a statistically significant decrease in lacrimal control in the surgical group within two to three months of denervation. Additionally, four participants in the surgical group experienced sensorineural hearing loss of 35 dB to 50 dB at 4000 Hz, and three participants reported tinnitus. However, due to the small number of participants and the design of the trials, the evidence for adverse effects was also considered very uncertain. In conclusion, the evidence from RCTs or quasi-RCTs regarding the use of surgery for the early management of Bell's palsy is of very low certainty. This evidence is insufficient to determine whether surgical intervention is beneficial or harmful. Further research on this topic is unlikely to be conducted, as most cases of Bell's palsy resolve spontaneously or with medical treatment.
